interviewQuestions.question: Explain out-of-order execution and why it matters.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd start from the motivation: an in-order pipeline is only as fast as its slowest stalled instruction. If an instruction stalls on a 200-cycle cache miss, every instruction fetched after it is stuck waiting behind it in program order — even instructions that are completely independent and have nothing to do with the stalled load. That's a huge amount of wasted execution capacity sitting idle for no reason other than program order.

Out-of-order (OoO) execution fixes this by letting instructions execute as soon as their **operands are ready**, not in the order they were fetched. Mechanically: an instruction decodes and dispatches into a **reservation station**, where it waits for any operands it still needs; those operands arrive via a broadcast bus (Tomasulo's common data bus) from whichever instruction produced them, whenever that happens to complete. Meanwhile, a separate structure — the **reorder buffer (ROB)** — tracks every in-flight instruction in original program order and only **commits** results (makes them architecturally visible) in that same order, which is exactly what keeps exceptions precise despite execution happening out of order underneath.

Concrete payoff: while one instruction sits blocked on a slow cache miss, several independent instructions behind it in the program can execute, complete, and sit ready in the ROB waiting their turn to commit — real measured IPC on OoO cores is routinely 2-4x higher than an equivalent in-order design on the same clock speed, purely from not wasting cycles behind stalls.

**Testing:** connecting the concrete motivation (stalls blocking unrelated work) to the actual mechanism (reservation stations plus in-order commit via the ROB), not just naming both separately.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: OoO execution motivation and mechanism

interviewQuestions.question: How does Tomasulo's algorithm resolve hazards without stalling the whole pipeline?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd describe the core trick as tagging values instead of waiting on register-file timing. In a naive design, an instruction needing an operand would have to wait until that operand is actually written to the register file and then read it back out — a slow round trip. Tomasulo's algorithm instead lets an instruction dispatch immediately into a reservation station holding either the operand's actual value (if already available) or a **tag** identifying which in-flight instruction will produce it.

When the producing instruction finishes execution, it broadcasts its result and its tag on the **common data bus (CDB)** in the same cycle — every reservation station currently waiting on that tag grabs the value simultaneously, the instant it's available, with no register-file round trip and no stall for the consumer. This is exactly how RAW hazards get resolved through data-driven wakeup rather than a scheduled wait.

The algorithm also effectively eliminates WAR and WAW hazards as a side effect: since each reservation station holds its own private copy of an operand (or its own tag) rather than sharing one register-file slot, two instructions that both happen to write the same architectural register never actually contend for the same physical storage the way a naive in-order design would force them to — this is the historical root of what later became explicit register renaming.

Concrete example: `MUL R1, R2, R3` followed by `ADD R4, R1, R5` — ADD's reservation station holds a tag for MUL's result instead of stalling; the moment MUL broadcasts on the CDB, ADD's station captures the value and ADD can issue that same cycle.

**Testing:** understanding tag-based broadcast as the actual mechanism resolving hazards, not just asserting 'it schedules dynamically.'
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Tomasulo's tag-broadcast mechanism

interviewQuestions.question: For a beginner: if instructions execute out of program order, how does the program still produce the correct result?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd separate two things that sound like they should be the same but aren't: the order instructions **execute** in, and the order their results become **visible** in. Out-of-order execution only reorders the first one.

The hardware tracks true data dependences carefully — an instruction can only execute once its actual input values are ready, and those values can only come from instructions that produced them, so genuine dependence chains (RAW hazards) are never violated; the machine simply finds independent instructions to run in the gaps rather than sitting idle. What changes is the *timing* of when different independent instructions finish relative to each other — not whether any instruction's inputs are correct when it runs.

The second half of the answer is the reorder buffer: even though instructions finish executing in whatever order their dependencies allow, their results are held in the ROB and only **committed** — written to the architecturally visible register file and memory — strictly in original program order. So from the perspective of anything outside the CPU (the OS, a debugger, another core watching memory), the program's effects appear exactly as if it ran in program order, one instruction at a time — the reordering is entirely invisible outside the core, which is precisely the guarantee that makes OoO safe to use without changing how software is written.

**Testing:** distinguishing execution order (reordered) from commit/visibility order (preserved), the core idea that makes OoO transparent to software.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Why reordering execution doesn't break correctness
